The merge sort implementation in CSLib (here) uses a custom TimeM complexity monad in order to track ticks performed by the algorithm and be able to formulate and prove assertions about its complexity.

This is an interesting approach as otherwise extensionality of functions prevents inspecting their inner behavior. However, this is an intrusive approach as one has to modify the function (to explicitly call the tick routine through the ✓ syntax) and its return type (to make the time attribute available).

I was wondering if this has an impact on the intermediate C code generated by Lean and, if yes, on the generated executable after compilation?

This will surely generate worse C code; I doubt the compiler can optimize out the counting. If your goal is to write code that is performant when compiled to C, then you should probably

  1. Write the pure function in the optimal way
  2. Write the ideal algorithmic version in TimeM / FreeM
  3. Prove that 1 and 2 coincide on what they compute

Eric Wieser said :

I doubt the compiler can optimize out the counting.

I know nothing about compilation, but I find it upsetting if neither the transpilation phase nor the compilation can detect and erase that superfluous piece of data / logic. I'm curious if there would be a more explicit way to trigger that kind of erasure maybe?

The compiler is not aware of your intent. In both TimeM and Prog approaches that Eric mentions, you have to express this intent in some way. In TimeM this is by run and in Prog this is done by interpreting the program systematically through the user provided model. The compiler doesn’t know what a user intended to do when using either monad. In practice the C compiler might just eliminate the ticks as dead code.

Of course the compiler cannot "read my mind", but since usage of the time part of the computation should be erased with the proofs and become dead code it would not be too surprising to me (but again, I know nothing about compilation) that there could be some option so that it is erased in some way.
The compiler cannot do that without knowing how you use the result of the ticks.

Maybe a better argument would be that if you have a callstack of TimeM functions, the compiler would need to know to emit an optimized copy of each one for the case where the top-level caller discards the tick count. Maybe with heavy inlining this would work, but the compiler would need to be able to move this "discard the ticks" operation through loops and complex recursions structures, which seems rather unlikely.
Just speculation but would it be possible for Lean tooling to erase TimeM and map to a pure function? Maybe with annotations.
This is essentially what run already does
I mean code generation with TimeM erased.

I've been following the TimeM/FreeM development and played with the concepts a bit and found this:

Code

@[expose] def StateT' (σ σ': Prop) (m : Type u → Type v) (α : Type u) : Type v :=
  σ → m (@Subtype α (fun _ => σ'))

@[expose, reducible]
def StateM' (σ σ': Prop) (α : Type u) : Type u := StateT' σ σ' Id α

variable {σ σ' : Prop} {m : Type u → Type v}
variable [Monad m] {α β : Type u}

@[always_inline, inline, expose]
protected def StateT'.pure (a : α) : StateT' σ σ m α :=
  fun s => pure (.mk a s)

@[always_inline, inline, expose]
protected def StateT'.bind {σ''} (x : StateT' σ σ' m α) (f : α → StateT' σ' σ'' m β) : StateT' σ σ'' m β :=
  fun s => do let (.mk a s) ← x s; f a s

@[always_inline, inline, expose]
protected def StateT'.map (f : α → β) (x : StateT' σ σ' m α) : StateT' σ σ' m β :=
  fun s => do let (.mk a s) ← x s; pure (.mk (f a) s)


@[always_inline, inline, expose]
protected def StateT'.modifyGet (f : σ → (@Subtype α (fun _ => σ'))) : StateT' σ σ' m α :=
  fun s => pure (f s)


inductive Bumpable : Nat → Prop where
| bump {n : Nat} (b : Bumpable n) : Bumpable (n+1)


set_option trace.compiler.ir.result true in -- no wrappers in IR :)
def test (a : Nat) {c : Nat} : StateM' (Bumpable c) (Bumpable (c+1)) Nat :=
  let comp := StateT'.modifyGet (fun s => .mk (a+1) (.bump s))
  comp.bind (fun r => .pure (r+1))


inductive IsLegalComp (α : Type u) : (s : Nat) → (e : Nat) → StateM' (Bumpable s) (Bumpable e) α → Prop where
| pure {s : Nat} {a : α} : IsLegalComp α s s (.pure a)
| bind {s i e : Nat}
    {x : StateM' (Bumpable s) (Bumpable i) α} {f : α → StateM' (Bumpable i) (Bumpable e) α}
    (lx : IsLegalComp α s i x) (lf : ∀ a, IsLegalComp α i e (f a))
    : IsLegalComp α s e (.bind x f)
| bump {s : Nat} (f : (Bumpable s) → (@Subtype α (fun _ => (Bumpable (s+1)))))
    : IsLegalComp α s (s+1) (.modifyGet f)


example (a : Nat) {c: Nat} : IsLegalComp _ c (c+1) (test a) := by
  dsimp [test]
  apply IsLegalComp.bind
  · apply IsLegalComp.bump
  · intro a
    apply IsLegalComp.pure


example {s e x} (h : IsLegalComp α s e x) [hmm : Inhabited α]
  : s ≤ e := by
  induction h with
  | pure => apply Nat.le_refl
  | bind hx hf  ihx ihf =>
      apply Nat.le_trans  ihx
      exact ihf Inhabited.default
  | bump f => apply Nat.le_succ

The idea was to have a tick counting state monad for which the generated IR isn't affected, and to achieve this by wrapping the counter in Prop, since the compiler ignores proofs. I tried to adapt StateM to have a Prop state, and ended up parametrising with two props, as otherwise the state couldn't really change at bind.
Long story short, in the above test has an IR in which the "monad" doesn't appear, and we still have operations counting in the definition.

Then there is the issue of needing to talk about program structure when proving lower bounds. A solution could be to define an inductive predicate that specifies what a "legal" program must look like. On can then prove that a given program is legal, and prove statements about any legal programs, as in the examples above. This doesn't solve the issue of "sneeking in pure values" though.

In any case, I hope this was interesting :smiley:
You might be interested in docs#Erased. So I guess TimeM (Erased Nat) α is an option
Probably we need the missing Add instance

Likewise for Prog, you just use Erased Nat as the cost type of your model.

@Yves Jäckle : this is essentially the idea that cslib#376 attempted, except they used arbitrary monads, and non-prop state. The issue is they also had to create the inductive type of valid programs for lower bounds. Which was … the free monad. I just used the free monad all the way. The so-called “monad” polymorphism of the aforementioned PR is just model polymorphism in my approach.
The advantage of monad polymorphism is that the compiler runs separately on each instantiation, and so you can genuinely get an efficient program with no hint of instrumentation.

@Eric Wieser free monads are monad polymorphic already. They are functor polymorphic.

separately, algorithms in both free monad PRs are transformed into Id monad* for execution so there is no instrumentation to erase.

*although now I have extended it locally to arbitrary monads to allow stateful query progs
Sure, but they're not polymorphic to the compiler in a way that is supported by @[specialize]
But that isn’t important when the object actually being run is an Id monad program with no ticks is it?

The object actually being run is a sequence of lean IR instructions. The question is whether you can persuade the compiler to reduce FreeM.liftM to the instructions it would have emitted had you used the Id monad directly. Maybe the answer is yes after adding more attributes, but I think it's no for the version currently in cslib.

So I kept exploring and now have this:

Code

/-- The factorial -/
def fac : Nat → Nat
  | 0 => 1
  | n+1 => (n+1) * fac n

#eval fac 3

/--
`LegalCompOfFac n x c` says: given input `n` and output `x`, the computation took `c` time
-/
inductive LegalCompOfFac : Nat → Nat → Nat → Prop  where
/-- Computing the input costs nothing-/
| input {input} : LegalCompOfFac input input 0
/-- Computing a literal costs nothing-/
| literal {input} : LegalCompOfFac input 1 0
/-- Computing an addition requires computing both terms and 1 addition-/
| add {input c q a b}
    (ha : LegalCompOfFac input a c) (hb : LegalCompOfFac input b q)
    : LegalCompOfFac input (a+b) (c + q + 1)
/-- Computing a multiplicaiton requires computing both factors and 1 addition-/
| mul {input c q a b}
    (ha : LegalCompOfFac input a c) (hb : LegalCompOfFac input b q)
    : LegalCompOfFac input (a*b) (c + q + 1)
/-- If we can compute `a` in `c` time given input `input - 1`,
we can makes a subtraction to the input (1 cost), then run that computation
to get a computation of `a` in `c+1` total time -/
| dec_input {input c a}
    (ha : LegalCompOfFac (input - 1) a c)
    : LegalCompOfFac input a (c + 1)


example (n : Nat) : LegalCompOfFac n (fac n) (2*n) := by
  induction n with
  | zero =>
    dsimp [fac]
    apply LegalCompOfFac.literal
  | succ n ih =>
    dsimp [fac]
    rw [show 2*(n+1) = 0 + (2*n + 1) + 1 from by grind]
    apply @LegalCompOfFac.mul (n+1) 0 (2*n + 1) (n+1) (fac n)
    · apply LegalCompOfFac.input
    · apply LegalCompOfFac.dec_input
      rw [Nat.add_one_sub_one]
      exact ih


example (f c : Nat → Nat)
  (hl : ∀ n, LegalCompOfFac n (f n) (c n)) (hf : ∀ n, f n = fac n)
  : ∀ n, c n ≥ 2*n := by
    sorry

Turns out the approach with the inductive type can be used to describe non monadic functions too.
I guess the solution to "sneeking in pure values" could be to have only have explicit constants in the inductive type, with other free variables either representing the input, or being given the hypothesis of "legality". Or one could have a dedicated type just for legal standard arithmetic operations.
Does anyone want to give a proof r disproof of the sorry ?

Never mind, the approach is fails in many ways :sad: . In particular, one can "cheat" by lifting:

Code

inductive LegalArithComp : Nat → Nat → Nat → Prop  where
| input {input} : LegalArithComp input input 0
| literal {input} : LegalArithComp input 1 0
| op {input c q a b} {op : Nat → Nat → Nat}
    (hop : op ∈ [Nat.add, Nat.mul, Nat.sub])
    (ha : LegalArithComp input a c) (hb : LegalArithComp input b q)
    : LegalArithComp input (op a b) (c + q + 1)
| letBind {input c q a} {b : Nat → Nat}
    (ha : LegalArithComp input a c) (hb : ∀ x, LegalArithComp x (b x) q) -- lose input ...
    : LegalArithComp input (let tmp := a ; b tmp) (c + q)

def testLift (n : Nat) :=
  (n+1) * (n+1)

example {n} : LegalArithComp n (testLift n) 2 := by
  have : testLift n = (let tmp := n+1 ; (fun x => x*x) tmp) := rfl
  rw [this]
  apply @LegalArithComp.letBind n 1 1 (n+1) (fun x => x*x)
  · apply @LegalArithComp.op n 0 0 n 1 Nat.add (by grind)
    · apply LegalArithComp.input
    · apply LegalArithComp.literal
  · intro x
    apply @LegalArithComp.op x 0 0 x x Nat.mul (by grind)
    all_goals apply LegalArithComp.input

Alternatively, one has to interpret the predicate as meaning that the computation is up to type theoretic reductions, even if the generated code is different (in the presence of certain optimizations)...

Sneaking in pure computation is not really a big deal. In fact it’s something we want to be able to do. The algorithm itself will always be part of the spec that must be checked by human reviewers. My goal is partly to make this review easier.

What I introduced with Prog is a structural way of reasoning about algorithmic complexity that removes the arbitrariness of placing ticks and costs for those ticks, and lets us reason about models.

One idea that Sandy Maguire had in polysymy was to Church-encode the Freer monad. Sandy never quite managed to make the abstraction zero-cost (see here); however, this way of formulating the Freer monad proved significantly cheaper than the usual concrete ADT approach. And Lean has a different IR than Haskell, so an optimization might be possible here.
